reason: Graphs of V against r (slope is dV/dr) and of dr/dt against r show why the chain rule divides the rates.

scenes.title: The slope of V against r
scenes.purpose: See that dV/dr is the gradient of the curve V = (11/3)πr³, and that it grows like r².

steps.text: The cylinder gives $\pi r^2\times 3r=3\pi r^3$ and the hemisphere gives $\frac{2}{3}\pi r^3$. Together $V=\frac{11}{3}\pi r^3$, the curve drawn. This earns the M1 and the B1.
Slide $r$ and watch the tangent at $P$. Its gradient is $\frac{\mathrm{d}V}{\mathrm{d}r}=11\pi r^2$, which matches the live reading. This is the final M1 for differentiating $kr^3$ to get $3kr^2$.
The curve is written as one power $r^3$ before differentiating. Differentiating the factors separately would not give this gradient.

guide.what_you_see: The graph of the volume $V$ of the cylinder-plus-hemisphere solid against its radius $r$, which is the curve $V=\frac{11}{3}\pi r^3$, with a point $P$ on it and the tangent at $P$. The tangent's gradient is $\frac{\mathrm{d}V}{\mathrm{d}r}$, the quantity the question asks for.

legend.meaning: The curve $V=\frac{11}{3}\pi r^3$, the total volume of the cylinder (height $3r$) and the hemisphere, drawn with $r$ along the horizontal axis.
The point on the curve with horizontal coordinate equal to the slider value $r$, so its height is the current volume $\frac{11}{3}\pi r^3$.
The tangent to $V$ at $P$; its gradient is $\frac{\mathrm{d}V}{\mathrm{d}r}=11\pi r^2$ at that radius.
A live text box at the top of the graph giving the current $r$, the volume $V$ and the tangent's gradient.

interact.do: Drag the slider from $0.3$ up to $3$, pausing at $r=1$, $r=2$ and $r=3$.
interact.watch: $P$ moves along the curve and the tangent steepens. At $r=1$ the gradient is $11\pi\approx 34.6$ and $V\approx 11.5$. At $r=2$ the gradient is $44\pi\approx 138.2$ and $V\approx 92.2$. At $r=3$ the gradient is $99\pi\approx 311.0$ and $V=99\pi$. Doubling $r$ makes the gradient four times as large, because it grows like $r^2$.

question_link.text: The curve $V$ is the total volume: the cylinder $\pi r^2\times 3r=3\pi r^3$ (first M1) plus the hemisphere $\frac{2}{3}\pi r^3$ (B1), giving $\frac{11}{3}\pi r^3$. The gradient of the tangent $T$ at $P$ is $\frac{\mathrm{d}V}{\mathrm{d}r}=11\pi r^2$, which is what the final M1 for differentiating $kr^3$ to $3kr^2$ produces.

read_off: The text box reads the slider radius $r$ in cm, the volume $V=\frac{11}{3}\pi r^3$ in $\mathrm{cm^3}$, and the gradient $11\pi r^2$, which is $\frac{\mathrm{d}V}{\mathrm{d}r}$ at that radius and matches the slope of $T$.

scenes.title: How fast r grows when the volume grows steadily
scenes.purpose: See that dr/dt equals 40 divided by dV/dr, so r grows more slowly as r gets larger.

steps.text: With $\frac{\mathrm{d}V}{\mathrm{d}t}=40$ and $\frac{\mathrm{d}V}{\mathrm{d}r}=11\pi r^2$, the chain rule gives $\frac{\mathrm{d}r}{\mathrm{d}t}=\frac{40}{11\pi r^2}$, the curve drawn. You divide, so the curve falls as $r$ grows. This is the M1.
Set $r=2$: $\frac{\mathrm{d}r}{\mathrm{d}t}=\frac{40}{44\pi}=\frac{10}{11\pi}\approx 0.289$ cm s$^{-1}$. This is the A1, with units.
Multiplying the rates would give about $5530$, far off the graph. Inverting the fraction would give $3.46$, which is seconds per cm. Both are clearly not a value on this curve.

guide.what_you_see: A decreasing curve showing how fast the radius $r$ of the cylinder-and-hemisphere solid grows, $\frac{\mathrm{d}r}{\mathrm{d}t}$, at each value of $r$ when the volume increases at $40\,\mathrm{cm^3\,s^{-1}}$. A point on the curve and a vertical line mark the chosen radius. The horizontal axis is $r$ (cm) and the vertical axis is $\frac{\mathrm{d}r}{\mathrm{d}t}$ (cm s$^{-1}$).

legend.meaning: The curve $\frac{\mathrm{d}r}{\mathrm{d}t}=\frac{40}{11\pi r^2}$, which is $40$ divided by $\frac{\mathrm{d}V}{\mathrm{d}r}=11\pi r^2$ from part (a). Here $r$ is drawn along the $x$-axis.
The point on the curve at the current slider radius, with height equal to the rate at which $r$ is increasing at that radius.
A vertical guide line at the current value of $r$, joining the axis to $P$.

interact.do: Drag the slider between $0.6$ and $3.5$, and set it to $2$ for the value the question asks about.
interact.watch: $P$ and the vertical line move along the curve. The curve is steep for small $r$ and flattens as $r$ grows, so $r$ grows more slowly for a bigger solid. At $r=2$ the height is $\frac{10}{11\pi}\approx 0.289$.

question_link.text: The curve is $\frac{\mathrm{d}r}{\mathrm{d}t}=40\div\frac{\mathrm{d}V}{\mathrm{d}r}$, the division that earns the M1 using your $\frac{\mathrm{d}V}{\mathrm{d}r}$ from part (a). The height of $P$ at $r=2$ is the answer the A1 asks for, $0.289\,\mathrm{cm\,s^{-1}}$.

read_off: The live label 'When r = ..., dr/dt = ... cm/s' gives the current radius in cm and the rate at which $r$ is increasing in $\mathrm{cm\,s^{-1}}$. At $r=2$ it reads about $0.289$, the answer to the question.
